Stage 3 · Grammar

Rules: what you must, may and need not do

Three questions: is it necessary, is it allowed, is it possible?

Read these four sentences about Ed’s first job.
  • He had to turn up for work on time.
  • He didn’t have to take much responsibility.
  • He didn’t need to get up early, because the van opened at eleven.
  • When he wanted to, he could even take a day off.
Which two sentences mean the same thing?
The two negatives in this lesson mean opposite things, and that is the whole point.

This group of modals expresses how free somebody is to act. Must and have to impose an obligation. Can, may and be allowed to grant permission. Don’t have to and needn’t remove an obligation. Mustn’t and can’t forbid. Four boxes, and the entire lesson depends on keeping them apart.

The critical pair is mustn’t and don’t have to. These look like the same negative but are opposites. You mustn’t use your phone forbids it absolutely. You don’t have to use your phone says it is entirely optional. A learner who treats them as interchangeable will regularly say the reverse of what they mean, sometimes with real consequences at work.

The distinction between must and have to is subtler and concerns the source of the obligation. Must normally means the speaker feels the necessity themselves: I must stop checking my phone at work. Have to normally points to an external rule, law, job or authority: He had to turn up on time because that was the job. In modern spoken English have to is by far the more common of the two; must survives mainly in written notices, formal rules, and strong personal resolutions.

There is also a purely structural fact worth knowing in advance: must has no past and no future form. Whatever the source of the obligation, the past is had to and the future is will have to. And separately, must has a second, unrelated meaning — deduction, as in You must be tired — which belongs to Lesson 26 and should not be mixed with obligation here.

Before you look at the table: the table below is organised into the four boxes — necessary, forbidden, optional, permitted. Before you read the forms, make sure you can put mustn’t and don’t have to into two different boxes.
Necessary, allowed, or possible?
MeaningPositiveNegativeExample
It is necessaryhave to · must You have to wear a uniform.
It is not necessary don’t have to · don’t need toYou don’t have to wear a tie.
It is forbidden mustn’t · can’t · aren’t allowed toYou mustn’t use the phone for private calls.
It is allowedcan · be allowed to You are allowed to take a day off.
The pair that changes everything
SentenceWhat it really means
You mustn’t be late.Being late is forbidden. Do not do it.
You don’t have to be early.Being early is optional. Do it if you like.

Must and have to are close, but not identical. Must usually comes from the speaker (I must call her); have to usually comes from a rule outside the speaker (I have to wear a badge). In everyday English, have to is more common.

Only have to has a past. There is no past form of must: not I musted but I had to.

The mistake to avoid. No to after must or can: not You must to go but You must go. And have to takes do in questions and negatives: Do you have to work Saturdays?

Permission, formally. Be allowed to works in every tense, which can does not: We weren’t allowed to leave, You’ll be allowed to choose — exactly like be able to in Lesson 7 recycled.

Now say it. Three rules from your own life, one of each kind.

Say them out loud: one I have to…, one I don’t have to…, one I’m not allowed to…Say all three to your teacher.Say all three to your partner, then listen to theirs.

Full grammar reference — obligation, permission and possibility — must, have to, can, be allowed to

What it is

This set of modals and semi-modals expresses how free somebody is to act. Must and have to impose an obligation; can, be allowed to and may grant permission; don’t have to and needn’t remove an obligation; mustn’t and can’t forbid. Getting the negative pair right matters more than anything else here.

What it means, and what it does

The single most important contrast in this lesson is that mustn’t and don’t have to are opposites, not synonyms. You mustn’t use your phone forbids it. You don’t have to use your phone says it is optional. Learners who treat them as the same thing produce sentences that mean the reverse of what they intend, which is why this pair is drilled separately at every level.

When and why we use it

This group of modals expresses how free somebody is to act. Must and have to impose an obligation. Can, may and be allowed to grant permission. Don’t have to and needn’t remove an obligation. Mustn’t and can’t forbid. Four boxes, and the entire lesson depends on keeping them apart.

The critical pair is mustn’t and don’t have to. These look like the same negative but are opposites. You mustn’t use your phone forbids it absolutely. You don’t have to use your phone says it is entirely optional. A learner who treats them as interchangeable will regularly say the reverse of what they mean, sometimes with real consequences at work.

The distinction between must and have to is subtler and concerns the source of the obligation. Must normally means the speaker feels the necessity themselves: I must stop checking my phone at work. Have to normally points to an external rule, law, job or authority: He had to turn up on time because that was the job. In modern spoken English have to is by far the more common of the two; must survives mainly in written notices, formal rules, and strong personal resolutions.

There is also a purely structural fact worth knowing in advance: must has no past and no future form. Whatever the source of the obligation, the past is had to and the future is will have to. And separately, must has a second, unrelated meaning — deduction, as in You must be tired — which belongs to Lesson 26 and should not be mixed with obligation here.

Typical situations

You need these forms for describing rules at work and at school, explaining what a job requires, asking for and giving permission, reading signs and regulations, and telling somebody what is and is not allowed.

  • Obligation from the speaker — must — the speaker themselves feels or imposes the need.I must remember to turn up on time.
  • Obligation from outside — have to — a rule, a law, a job, somebody else’s decision.He had to be reliable and turn up for work on time.
  • Prohibition — mustn’t or can’t — it is forbidden.You mustn’t tell anyone about this.
  • No obligation — don’t have to or needn’t — it is not necessary, you may choose.You don’t have to bring your own tools.
  • Permission — can (neutral), may (formal), be allowed to (about rules).Staff are allowed to take an hour for lunch.
  • Asking for permission — Can I…? / Could I…? / May I…? in rising order of formality.Could I leave twenty minutes early today?

How it differs from similar structures

mustn’t = it is forbidden · don’t have to = it is not necessary. You mustn’t tell her (keep it secret) vs You don’t have to tell her (it is up to you).
must = the obligation comes from the speaker · have to = the obligation comes from outside. I must stop eating so much sugar (my decision) vs I have to wear a uniform (the company’s rule).

How to build it

Obligation: subject + must / have to / has to / had to + base verb
Prohibition: subject + mustn’t / can’t + base verb
No obligation: subject + don’t / doesn’t / didn’t have to + base verb
Permission: subject + can / may / am / is / are allowed to + base verb
AffirmativeYou must wear a helmet. · She has to work Saturdays. · We are allowed to park here.
Negative — forbiddenYou mustn’t park here. · You can’t take photos.
Negative — not necessaryYou don’t have to park here. · She doesn’t have to work Saturdays.
QuestionDo I have to book? · Are we allowed to film? · Can I ask something?
Pasthad to (obligation) · didn’t have to (no obligation) · was / were allowed to (permission). Must has no past.
Futurewill have to · won’t have to · will be allowed to

Saying it — contractions and stress

  • have to is normally pronounced /hæf tə/ and has to /hæs tə/ — with an f and an s sound, not a v or a z. Learners who say /hæv tuː/ sound noticeably non-native here.
  • must loses its t before a consonant: must be sounds like ‘mus’ be’.
  • mustn’t is pronounced /ˈmʌsnt/ — the first t is silent.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • Must has no past and no future form. Use had to for the past and will have to for the future, whatever the source of the obligation.
  • In modern English, have to is far more common than must in speech. Must survives mainly in written rules, notices and strong personal resolutions.
  • Needn’t + base verb is a British alternative to don’t have to: You needn’t come. It is not the same as mustn’t.
  • Be allowed to is the only one of these that easily becomes passive-like in reports: Children are not allowed to enter. It is the natural choice when you are describing an institution’s rules.
  • May for permission is formal and often written; can is the everyday spoken form. May also has a second, unrelated meaning — probability — which is Lesson 11.
  • Must has a second use, deduction (You must be tired), which is covered in Lesson 26. Do not mix the two meanings.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • You don’t have to smoke here. → You mustn’t smoke here.If it is forbidden, use mustn’t; don’t have to makes it optional.
  • Yesterday I must work late. → Yesterday I had to work late.Must has no past form.
  • She must to arrive at nine. → She must arrive at nine.Modals are followed by the base verb with no to.
  • Do you must book a table? → Do you have to book a table?Must forms questions by inversion, not with do; in practice have to is used.
  • We are not allowed take photos. → We are not allowed to take photos.Be allowed always keeps to before the verb.
  • He hasn’t to come. → He doesn’t have to come.Have to forms its negative with do / does.

More examples in context

  • personal obligationI must stop checking my phone at work.
  • external ruleApplicants have to hold a school leaver’s certificate.
  • past obligationIn the burger van he had to turn up on time and be polite.
  • prohibitionYou mustn’t share the password with anyone.
  • prohibition, spokenSorry, you can’t bring food into the studio.
  • no obligationThe job is flexible — you don’t have to start at nine.
  • no obligation, pastLuckily we didn’t have to pay for the second night.
  • permissionStaff are allowed to work from home twice a week.
  • asking permissionCould I take Friday off, if the schedule allows it?
  • future obligationIf you want the promotion you’ll have to supervise a team.

A tip for remembering it

Sort every sentence into one of four boxes before you choose the form: necessary (must / have to), forbidden (mustn’t / can’t), optional (don’t have to / needn’t), permitted (can / may / be allowed to). The two negatives are in different boxes — that is the whole lesson.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Must = obligation the speaker feels; have to = obligation imposed from outside.
  2. Mustn’t = forbidden. Don’t have to = not necessary. They are opposites.
  3. Must has no past or future: use had to and will have to.
  4. Modals take the base verb with no to; have to and be allowed to keep the to.
  5. Have to makes questions and negatives with do / does / did.
  6. For permission: can (everyday), may (formal), be allowed to (rules and institutions).

Stage 5 · Main input

Faking it

Four weeks to learn a job, and a panel of judges who have to spot the beginner.

Before you read: a television programme trains people with no experience for four weeks, then asks professionals to spot them.

What do you think gives the fakes away?

Choose one. Paragraph E tells you what the judges actually say.

Faking it

A television programme sends people with no experience into a job for four weeks, then asks a panel of professionals to spot them. What separates the ones who survive from the ones who don’t is rarely what you would expect.

AThe idea behind the programme is simple and slightly cruel. Producers take somebody with no experience in a particular job — a chef, a chauffeur, a fitness instructor — and give them four weeks with an expert. At the end, they must take part in a contest against real professionals, and a panel of judges has to decide which one is faking it. If the judges cannot tell, the newcomer wins.

BEd worked in a burger van before the programme found him. He had to be reliable and turn up for work on time; he had to be reasonably pleasant to customers; and that, more or less, was the job. He did not have to take much responsibility, because his boss dealt with the money. Four weeks later he was expected to run a professional kitchen. “Nobody tells you,” he said afterwards, “that in a real kitchen you must work to very precise times. Thirty seconds is a long time.”

CThis is where most candidates struggle, and it is not usually the technical skill that defeats them. You can teach somebody to crack an egg, flip it and get it onto a plate. You cannot teach them, in four weeks, to multitask under pressure while five other people are shouting. A chef must plan several dishes at once, hold the whole schedule in their head, and think ahead constantly. Candidates who set goals for each shift tend to survive; those who simply react do not.

DThe social rules are just as hard. Ed was shocked to realise that he could not say please and thank you all the time if he wanted the team to respect him — in a busy kitchen, a short instruction is not rudeness, it is efficiency. In other jobs the opposite applies. A chauffeur may not start a conversation with a passenger unless the passenger starts it first, and is not allowed to comment on anything they overhear. Every workplace has rules like these, and none of them are written down anywhere.

EJudges say the giveaway is almost never a technical mistake. It is confidence in the wrong place: the candidate who explains too much, apologises too often, or checks the time. One judge put it bluntly. “A professional does not have to think about how they look. That is the difference, and you can see it in about ninety seconds.”

FPerhaps the most useful thing the programme reveals is what a job actually consists of. We describe work in terms of qualifications and technique, but for four weeks these candidates discover something else: that most of a job is behaviour. You have to know when to speak, when to be quiet, what you are allowed to touch, and what nobody will ever explain to you. Some of them go back to their old lives afterwards. A surprising number do not.
